questions.question: In case length xs of { 0 -> "empty"; _ -> "has elements" }, what exactly is being pattern-matched — xs itself, or something else?
options: xs itself is matched directly against 0 and _
length xs is evaluated first, producing an Int, and that Int is what gets matched against the patterns 0 and _
This is invalid syntax, since case can only inspect a bare argument, not a whole expression like length xs
0 and _ are matched against each other, not against anything from xs
questions.explanation: case's expression slot accepts any expression, not just a bare variable. length xs is evaluated to some Int, and it is that Int — not the list xs — that the patterns 0 and _ are compared against.
optionFeedback: xs is a list, and 0 is an Int pattern — they are not even the same type. What is actually matched is length xs's result, an Int.
Correct — this is exactly the advantage case has over equation-level pattern matching: the thing being matched can be any expression, computed first, not only a function's own argument.
This is valid, ordinary case syntax — case's whole point, as the intro to this lesson states, is inspecting something that is 'not one of the function's arguments'.
Patterns are matched against the case expression's value, never against each other — 0 and _ are two alternative patterns competing for the same one value.

questions.question: case alternatives are written with ->, not =. Why does that distinction matter if you accidentally write case x of { 0 = 1; ... }?
options: It does not matter; Haskell accepts either symbol in a case alternative

-> and = mean different things in Haskell's grammar; = defines an equation's right-hand side, while -> is specifically the arrow used inside case (and later, lambdas), so using = there is a parse error, not just a style mistake
= is required only for the first alternative, and -> for the rest
case alternatives never need any arrow or equals sign at all
questions.explanation: -> and = belong to different syntactic constructs in Haskell. A case alternative's shape is always pattern -> result. Writing 0 = 1 instead of 0 -> 1 is not a valid case alternative at all, and GHC reports a parse error rather than silently accepting it.
optionFeedback: They are not interchangeable — see the Common errors table later in this lesson, which lists this exact mistake as a parse error.
Every alternative uses the same arrow -> consistently; there is no special first-alternative rule.
Each alternative needs its own -> connecting the pattern to its result; without it, the alternative is not valid syntax.

questions.question: compareCounts builds case (a > b, a == b) of ... rather than case a of .... What does building the tuple (a > b, a == b) actually accomplish?
options: Nothing beyond convenience — the tuple could be left out and the alternatives would still work the same way
It packages two separate Boolean tests into one value, so a single case expression can select among three outcomes using both results at once, instead of needing a nested case or extra guards
It converts a and b into a single number before comparing
It is required syntax — case can only scrutinise tuples, never a single expression
questions.explanation: case can only pattern-match on the one expression written after case. Bundling a > b and a == b into a tuple turns two separate Bool facts into one value with a fixed shape, which the three alternatives — (True, _), (False, True), (False, False) — can then match against together, distinguishing all three outcomes in one flat expression.
optionFeedback: Without the tuple, case would have only one Bool to inspect and could not distinguish three separate outcomes in one flat set of alternatives.
Correct — bundling both tests into one tuple value is exactly what lets one case expression discriminate three outcomes at once.
a > b and a == b are both already Bool values; nothing here converts a or b into a number.
Section 2 shows case scrutinising a bare Int (parity) and a String comparison earlier in the lesson — case works on any expression, not tuples exclusively.

questions.question: ticketPrice (True, True) matches the alternative (True, _) -> 6.50. Why does the wildcard in the second position not need to check whether it's actually the weekend?
options: Because the wildcard secretly still checks the value, just without producing a warning

Because the specification says a child's price is the same whether or not it's the weekend — the wildcard deliberately matches either True or False in that position, since the result does not depend on it
Because case alternatives are only allowed to inspect the first component of a tuple
Because ticketPrice (True, True) actually returns a different, incorrect price due to the wildcard
questions.explanation: The wildcard _ matches anything in that position without inspecting it. Since the child price is meant to be identical whichever day it is, (True, _) correctly captures both (True, True) and (True, False) with one alternative, rather than needing two separate identical-result alternatives.
optionFeedback: A wildcard genuinely ignores the value in that position; it performs no hidden check at all.
Correct — the wildcard is deliberate: the weekend flag doesn't affect a child's price, so one alternative correctly covers both possibilities for that position.
case alternatives can inspect every component of a tuple pattern, as (False, True) and (False, False) show later in the same function — the wildcard here is a choice, not a restriction.
6.50 is the documented, correct child price stated in the lesson's own example — this is not a bug.

questions.question: report embeds a case expression directly inside a ++ concatenation. Why is this possible for case but not for equation-level pattern matching (multiple function equations)?
options: It is not actually possible; report as written would not compile

case is an expression with a value and a type, so it can appear anywhere a value is expected — including as one operand of ++ — whereas equation-level patterns select which whole function equation runs, not a piece of one
++ is a special operator that only works with case expressions
report only works because compare n 0 happens to return a String
questions.explanation: case ... of ... is an ordinary expression, just like if ... then ... else — it reduces to one value with one type, so it can sit anywhere a value of that type is expected, including as the right operand of ++. Multiple function equations (like isVowel's ten equations in the previous lesson) work at a completely different level: they choose which entire equation body runs for a call, not a sub-expression within one body.
optionFeedback: report as written is valid, working Haskell — the ghci transcript above shows its actual output.
++ works with any two matching-typed lists; here both operands (the literal string and the case expression) evaluate to String, which is all ++ requires.
compare n 0 returns an Ordering (LT, EQ, or GT), not a String directly — it is the case expression as a whole, matching each Ordering to a String, that produces the String value passed to ++.

questions.question: In classifyHead, why is (y:_) written as one pattern with three attached guards, instead of writing three separate case alternatives like (y:_) | y < 0 -> ..., (y:_) | y == 0 -> ..., (y:_) | otherwise -> ... on three lines each starting with the pattern again?
options: Both forms are invalid; only a single un-guarded pattern is allowed per case

Guards attach to one pattern once, and the pattern match happens a single time; the three guard conditions then choose among results without needing to repeat and re-test the structural pattern (y:_) three separate times
case expressions cannot use guards at all, so this code would not compile
Repeating (y:_) three times would actually run faster
questions.explanation: Guards attached to one pattern are checked in order after that one pattern has already matched. This avoids restating and rematching the structural pattern (y:_) for each condition — the list is destructured into y and the tail once, and then the three Boolean conditions choose among results, exactly mirroring how guards work at the equation level.
optionFeedback: A pattern with attached guards is exactly what classifyHead uses, and it is valid, working Haskell as the transcript shows.
case expressions do support guards on their alternatives — that is precisely the feature this section introduces.
This is not a performance consideration covered by the course; the real reason is avoiding needless repetition of the same structural pattern.

questions.question: All four facIf, facPat, facGuard, and facCase above compute exactly the same results. Given that, why does the lesson still recommend facPat (pattern matching) specifically for this factorial specification?
options: Because pattern matching is always the fastest of the four forms

Because the base case in the specification is the literal value n = 0, and pattern matching is the form whose syntax most directly expresses "this literal value gets this result" — matching the shape of the specification, not just its correctness
Because facIf, facGuard, and facCase are all actually incorrect
Because case and guards cannot express recursion
questions.explanation: Correctness alone (all four compute 120 for facX 5) does not decide which form is best — the lesson's whole point is that the four forms should be chosen by matching the shape of the decision to the shape of the tool. Since the base case here is exactly one literal number, 0, pattern matching's literal-pattern syntax (facPat 0 = 1) states that fact more directly than a Boolean test (n == 0) does.
optionFeedback: The lesson does not claim any performance difference between the four forms; the recommendation is entirely about readability and fit to the specification's shape.
All four versions are correct, as the identical ghci output for facIf 5 through facCase 5 demonstrates.
case and guards both support recursion perfectly well — facGuard and facCase are themselves recursive, calling themselves in their otherwise/default cases.

questions.question: Suppose the factorial base case were instead specified as "n <= 1", not "n = 0". According to the Callout's habit, which form should now read best, and why?
options: Pattern matching still reads best, since patterns can match any condition
Guards, because n <= 1 is a range/inequality test rather than a single literal value, and guards are the form built specifically for range and compound conditions
if...then...else, because there are still only two outcomes overall
case, because case is always the most general and therefore always the best choice
questions.explanation: Patterns match literal values or structures — n = 0 fits a pattern exactly, but n <= 1 is a range (it covers both 0 and 1, and technically all values below 1), which patterns cannot express directly. Guards exist precisely for range and compound Boolean tests, which is why the Callout names 'ranges and compound tests' as pointing to guards.
optionFeedback: Patterns match literal values or structures, not inequalities — n <= 1 cannot be written as a literal pattern the way n = 0 can.

While the recursive function still has two logical branches (base case and recursive case), the recommendation here is about the shape of the base-case CONDITION specifically (a range) rather than a simple top-level count of outcomes.

case is not "always best" — the whole point of this comparison is that each form fits some decisions better than others; case is best for computed values or matches needed mid-expression, not for a plain range test on an argument.
